pass_a_gloss: He did not say 'first day'. For if he said first day, it was necessary for him to say also second day becoming. But it was necessary for him not to say first but 'one', so that through the 'one' he might show this day being cyclical, and the week being completed, and one existing. For the excess of the water being brought upon the face of the earth, for which reason the earth was also invisible and unformed, when the Master of all wished to make the invisible visible, then he froze the third part of the waters in the middle, and the third part he separated upwards. Taking up with his own power at the same time the solid part, and the third part he left below for use and enjoyment by men.
pass_b_english: He did not say 'first day,' because if he had said 'first day,' he would have been obliged to speak of a second day as well. Instead, he had to say not 'first' but 'one,' so that by the word 'one' he might show this day as cyclical, completing the week, yet itself remaining one. The excess of water was brought over the face of the earth, which is why the earth was invisible and unformed; when the Master of all wished to make the invisible visible, he froze a third of the waters in the middle, separated a third upward, lifted the solid part by his own power at the same time, and left a third below for human use and enjoyment.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between 'first' (πρώτην) and 'one' (μίαν), the cyclical nature of the week (κυκλουμένην), and the specific action of the Master (δεσπότης) regarding the waters. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
